To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the yolk fatty acid levels in eggs collected from regularly fed chickens were significantly different from the yolk fatty acids in the eggs collected from chickens fed with specially designed diets, but the yolk fatty levels in eggs from different sources within each group did not differ.

the yolk samples from the three regularly fed chickens were significantly different in terms of their fatty acid composition compared with the yolk samples collected from the three specially fed chickens (P <  0.05)
the fatty acid composition in egg yolk from chickens fed a diet containing linseed oil was significantly different from that in egg yolk samples collected from regularly fed chickens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fatty acid composition of hen egg yolks, and it is the first study of this nature to be conducted in Canada.
the composition of the fatty acids in hen's eggs from different sources, and the fatty acids are of nutritional importance to the human body.
fatty acids in eggs from different sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fatty acid levels in egg yolk are influenced by the diet of the chicken, but not the egg source.
the fatty acid profile of egg yolk is influenced by diet and season, and the fatty acid profile varies with egg source, but the variations are not statistically significant.
the fatty acid composition of the egg yolk is affected by the source of the eggs, but the effect is relatively minor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the egg yolk samples collected from regularly fed chickens had significantly higher (P<0.05) arachidonic (ARA) acid and lower (P <  0.05) linolenic acid (LNA) and docosahexoenoic acid (DHA) levels than the yolk samples from chickens fed special diets.
the fatty acid composition of hen egg yolks is influenced by the type of diet fed to chickens, but the influence is relatively small and not significant in all cases.
there is no significant difference in the fatty acid composition of eggs collected from different Canadian sources, and there is no significant seasonal effect on the fatty acid composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fatty acid levels of the egg yolks are not affected by the season of collection, the egg processing plant, and the egg producer.
the fatty acid composition of egg yolk can be manipulated by changing the chicken diet.
egg yolk samples collected from specially fed chickens contain higher amounts of omega-3 fatty acids, which are beneficial to human health.
